scripts.opening:opening:
[warmly] The Last Sunday.

[short pause] Sunday... 8 October 1871. Early afternoon. It has not rained for more than a week, [lightly] and a warm wind is blowing hard from the southwest. [short pause] Last night a fire on the West Side burned four blocks near the river, and the firemen are still at it. This morning's Tribune gave that fire three columns, and [amused] then went on to the city's big plans.

Nine stops: Lake Street, the Court House and the great hotel beside it, the grain market, a theatre getting ready for Monday night, the new stores of State Street, the Water Tower across the river, [short pause] and then, as the light goes, a small cottage on DeKoven Street. [short pause] Start on Lake Street.
scripts.stop:lake-street: [brightly] Lake Street at Clark, two in the afternoon. This was once the main street of Chicago. Until the mid-1860s it was 'the retail center of Chicago', and big wholesale houses still crowd the blocks between here and the river. Stone fronts with arched windows line both sides, with iron awnings over the walks and telegraph wires overhead. [short pause] Some of these buildings once stood lower. From 1859 George M. Pullman, the man who later built sleeping cars, raised whole blocks of brick and stone on jack-screws to the new street level, 'without even disturbing the operations of business inside'. [short pause] [softly] Today is Sunday, and the stores are shut. In this morning's Tribune a man who watches land prices said: '[amused] Every body seems to be swelled up with big schemes.' [short pause] One block south stands the grandest of those schemes, a hotel of white marble.
scripts.stop:sherman-house: [admiring] The Sherman House, at Clark and Randolph. Francis C. Sherman, who later served as mayor, built his first hotel on this corner in 1836-37. This one opened in July 1861: six storeys of 'the finest Athens marble, from the quarries at Lemont', with its main door on Clark Street through a two-storey porch. Its Randolph Street side looks out over the Court House square. [short pause] This week it has a famous guest. The conductor Theodore Thomas and his orchestra are staying here. [excited] Tomorrow night they open a season of ten concerts with 'his concert organization of sixty performers'. [short pause] Across Randolph Street, in the square, a bell of more than five tons hangs in the Court House tower.
scripts.stop:court-house: [measured] Court House Square, the whole block between Randolph, Clark, Washington and LaSalle. Its lawns, trees and fountain give it 'the appearance of a park', and an iron fence runs round it. The building in the middle holds almost every city and county office, 'from the jail in its basement to the mayor's quarters'. John M. Van Osdel designed it in 1853. Since then the city has added wings, a new clock and a bronze bell of 10,849 pounds. [short pause] Look up at the cupola. A spiral stair climbs to a balcony 120 feet high, the fire watchman's walk. [short pause] [quietly] Tonight the watchman on duty will be Mathias Schaffer, with his spy-glass. Below him is the telegraph office that sends the fire engines out. [short pause] Across LaSalle Street, the grain of the West is bought and sold.
scripts.stop:chamber: [measured] The Chamber of Commerce, on the southeast corner of Washington and LaSalle. Edward Burling designed it, and it opened on 30 August 1865. Charles Randolph, the president of the Board of Trade, gave the main speech that day. Inside is a great hall 'decorated with frescoes and paintings', and the business that matters most here is the Board's trade in grain. [short pause] [softly] The hall is quiet on a Sunday. LaSalle Street around it, a row of stone fronts under mansard roofs, has become 'the home of Insurance Companies and commission merchants', and the banks are moving in close. [short pause] Two blocks east, on Washington Street, workmen are busy even today, getting a theatre ready for Monday night.
scripts.stop:crosbys: [excited] Crosby's Opera House, on the north side of Washington Street between State and Dearborn. Uranus Crosby opened it in 1865, built by the architect W. W. Boyington: five storeys, a mansard roof, and statues of Painting, Sculpture, Music and Commerce over the arch. Shops fill the ground floor, and the theatre behind them seats three thousand. [short pause] All summer it has been done over, at a cost of about $80,000. This morning's Tribune said 'the whole house, gallery and all, is nearly sold for the first night.' [short pause] The first night is tomorrow, when Theodore Thomas opens the season. [short pause] [softly] Late this evening the gas will be lit inside for the first time, 'that its effects might be seen by gaslight'. [short pause] One block east is the newest shopping street in Chicago.
scripts.stop:state-street: [brightly] State Street at Washington. Four years ago this stretch held a frame house, an ale store and a furniture shop. [short pause] Then Potter Palmer, who had made his first fortune in trade, bought 'three-quarters of a mile of property along State Street south of Lake' to make it the city's great shopping street. On the northeast corner is the six-storey store of Field & Leiter, almost 150 feet long on State. Marshall Field and Levi Leiter moved here from Lake Street, and their clerks treat the ladies who shop here 'like guests rather than mere customers'. [short pause] A few blocks south is Palmer's own new hotel, the Palmer House. [short pause] [warmly] Across the river, on the North Side, the oldest and richest families live under great elms.
scripts.stop:water-tower: [admiring] The Water Tower, on Pine Street at Chicago Avenue, on the North Side. It was dedicated with a great celebration in 1867. Across the street, the Pumping Station draws clean water through a tunnel two miles out under the lake, far from the 'unspeakably polluted Chicago River'. W. W. Boyington, who also built Crosby's, designed both in 'castellated Gothic' stone. South of here, toward the river, are the homes of the old families, 'substantial and elegant, and shaded with grand elms'. [long pause] [seriously] For years the Board of Police and Fire Commissioners has warned that 'the water supply was insufficient'. [short pause] The whole city depends on this one set of pumps, [quietly] and the roof over them... is made of wood.
scripts.stop:saturday-ruins: [seriously] The east end of the Van Buren Street bridge, looking across to the West Side. Last night, between ten and eleven, a fire broke out in Lull & Holmes's planing mill on Canal Street, in a district insurance men call the 'Red Flash'. [short pause] By this afternoon four blocks and nearly a million dollars of property were gone. 'The piles of coal and lumber burned all day on Sunday', and thousands of people came to look. [short pause] Many of the firemen worked eighteen hours straight, until three o'clock this afternoon. They are 'nearly exhausted', and some of their equipment is damaged. [short pause] No rain has fallen for more than a week, and the wind is still strong from the southwest. [long pause] [softly] Ten blocks south, on DeKoven Street, a woman has milked her cows for the evening.
scripts.stop:dekoven: [quietly] 137 DeKoven Street, on the West Side, at dusk. This is a neighbourhood of small wooden houses, with 'wood shavings piled in every barn and under every house'. Patrick and Catherine O'Leary and their five children live in the back of this cottage, and rent the front to the McLaughlin family. [short pause] Behind it is a wooden barn, sixteen by twenty feet, its loft newly filled with hay. Inside are five cows, a calf and a horse. Catherine O'Leary sells milk to the neighbours. She milked at half past four, and at about seven she will feed the horse by the fence and shut him in. [short pause] [warmly] Tonight the McLaughlins have a party for a cousin just arrived from Ireland. Mr. McLaughlin is a fiddler, and there will be music. [long pause] [softly] The wind... has not dropped.
scripts.ending:the-barn:
[quietly] That night, at about nine, Daniel Sullivan, a drayman sitting on the sidewalk across DeKoven Street, saw fire in the O'Leary barn. [short pause] Within thirty minutes it 'was beyond the control of the Fire Department.' [short pause] In the Court House cupola Mathias Schaffer saw the glow, judged it too far away, and called the wrong alarm box. [long pause] [sadly] By Monday morning the Court House bell had fallen through the burning building. The Sherman House was 'one of the most complete wrecks of the night', and Crosby's Opera House never opened. At about three in the morning the pumping works became 'an utter wreck'. [short pause] Theodore Thomas 'was compelled to run for his life'.

[long pause] [wryly] According to legend, Mrs. O'Leary's cow kicked over a lamp. The historian A. T. Andreas wrote in 1885: 'There is no proof that Mrs. O'Leary is responsible for the fire.' [short pause] [softly] The Great Chicago Fire jaunt... begins in that barn.
